comparator.name: Global Communication Science
comparator.sourceNotes: UvA distinguishes the English Global Communication Science track from Dutch Communicatiewetenschap. The English study-programme table supplies 60 EC in each year. Year 1 contains seven compulsory courses (12+12+6+6+8+8+8 EC). Year 2 contains five 6-EC theory/research/practice courses, a 24-EC internationally oriented internship and a 6-EC internship case. Year 3 combines 30 EC of genuine open elective/minor/exchange space, one 6-EC communication-topic restricted elective, an 18-EC independent research project and 6 EC From Research to Impact. The named topic examples are not assigned as compulsory content; the 6-EC restricted choice is retained generically.

The broad option adds international relations, sociology, media history, environmental media and youth resilience.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The two accepted programmes differ in their public-media and organisational-audience purposes. A third health and sustainability communication programme would require more sustained communication study than the available direct subject courses support.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both examine changes in media and their social consequences. UCR follows American media and storytelling; UvA compares global digital production, algorithms, privacy and regulation.
No selected UCR course directly covers the specific UvA Communication Theme 2: Crises & Resilience requirement at its stated scope and credit weight; this distinct component remains visible.
UCR media and social psychology courses contribute to parts of the subject. No single selected course covers comparative communication-science theories across societies.
Both introduce research designs, data collection and statistical inference. UCR applies these skills in a general research project; UvA uses communication-science examples and SPSS.
Both develop experimental reasoning and analysis of human behaviour. UCR emphasises experimental design and statistical models; UvA also has students conduct a communication survey.
Both teach qualitative research design, interviews, focus groups and interpretation. UCR also covers ethnography and visual methods, while UvA focuses on intercultural communication research.
No selected UCR course directly covers the specific UvA Communication Research 2: Content Analysis requirement at its stated scope and credit weight; this distinct component remains visible.
No selected UCR course directly covers the specific UvA Communication Research 4: Statistical Reasoning requirement at its stated scope and credit weight; this distinct component remains visible.
No selected UCR course directly covers the specific UvA Communication Research Project requirement at its stated scope and credit weight; this distinct component remains visible.
Both study public communication about sustainability. UCR focuses on climate messages and participation in public debate; UvA also examines health across cultures.
Both study persuasive marketing and audience engagement. UCR develops consumer and brand strategy; UvA also studies entertainment, influencers and differences across markets.

No selected UCR course directly covers the specific UvA Communication Science in Practice 1: Global Case Studies requirement at its stated scope and credit weight; this distinct component remains visible.

notes.text: UvA requires a sequence in communication research, a 24-EC internship and an 18-EC independent research project. UCR builds related skills through media, rhetoric and empirical research courses. Its optional independent research sits outside the scheduled 180 EC.

audience.programmeDescription: Global Communication Science at the University of Amsterdam studies how media and communication shape people and societies across cultures. Students practise research methods and apply them through a supervised internship and an independent project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The first UCR option combines media, public communication and research methods. The second uses related tools to study how organisations understand and engage audiences.
